analysis.one_liner: Offers Senate candidates full public campaign financing if they give up large private donations.
analysis.headline: The Fair Elections Now Act, introduced by Senator Durbin with 24 Senate cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Rules Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a voluntary system where Senate candidates who collect a large number of small donations from state residents—between $5 and $100 each—could trade private big-dollar fundraising for public money: a base grant from a new Fair Elections Fund, a 4-to-1 match on small donations, and government-funded advertising vouchers. In exchange, participating candidates would have to swear off large contributions, personal wealth spending, and joint fundraising committees. It would also have forced broadcasters to sell campaign airtime to these candidates at a 20% discount, banned stations from bumping their ads, and sped up public disclosure of campaign finance reports.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates who can build support from many small donors but lack access to wealthy donors, party machines, or personal fortunes—typically challengers, outsiders, and candidates from less connected backgrounds. Voters gain a system in which senators are not indebted to large contributors, because participating candidates would be barred from taking big donations. Small-dollar donors gain a 4-to-1 match that multiplies their political voice.

how_it_helps.text: Candidates would qualify for public financing by gathering at least 2,000 qualifying contributions of $5 to $100 from state residents, plus 500 per congressional district—typing public funds to demonstrated grassroots support.

Participating candidates would receive a base allocation of $750,000 plus $150,000 per congressional district for the general election, a 4-to-1 federal match on qualified small-dollar contributions, and broadcast advertising vouchers worth $100,000 per congressional district.

The bill's stated purpose is to reduce the actual and perceived conflicts of interest created when senators rely on large contributions from private interests directly affected by federal legislation, and to free senators from constant fundraising.

Broadcasters would have to sell airtime to participating candidates at no more than 80% of the lowest unit charge, could not preempt ads the candidate has paid for, and could lose their license for denying candidates access on the same terms as the station's most favored advertiser.
FEC reports would have to be filed electronically and posted publicly within 24 hours instead of 48, giving voters faster access to who is funding campaigns.

analysis.who_pays: The program would be paid for from a new Fair Elections Fund. The bill expresses the Senate's view that the fund should be financed by a 0.5% tax on payments under federal contracts worth more than $10 million—capped at $500,000 per company per year—though this is a non-binding recommendation and the fund would otherwise depend on annual appropriations. Broadcasters bear the direct cost of mandatory discounts and new reporting duties.

drawbacks.text: The Fair Elections Fund depends on appropriations, and the proposed 0.5% tax on large federal contracts is only a 'sense of the Senate'—a non-binding suggestion—so the program's financing was not guaranteed and would require taxpayer money if the tax were never enacted.

The program is voluntary and covers only candidates who opt in, so wealthy self-funded candidates and outside groups could still spend without limit against publicly financed candidates—raising the question of whether grant levels would be sufficient in a post-spending-limits environment.
The bill regulates only Senate elections; House campaigns would remain entirely privately financed.
Mandatory discounted rates and voucher requirements impose direct costs on broadcasters, who would be compelled to sell advertising below their normal rates and report ad purchases to the government.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is a few hundred million dollars in public campaign funds per cycle, or a modest tax on large federal contractors, against reducing senators' dependence on large private contributions—an interest the bill itself argues costs taxpayers far more through legislative distortions. The main design weakness is that financing is not guaranteed and the program is voluntary, which could leave publicly funded candidates underfunded against unlimited outside spending. On balance, the bill offered a substantial public benefit with a small, defined cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which never took it up—no hearing, no markup, no floor vote—and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Durbin introduced the Fair Elections Now Act on March 31, 2009, along with Senator Arlen Specter.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration the day it was introduced; no further action appears in its record for the remainder of the 111th Congress.
The bill gathered 24 cosponsors: 22 of 58 Senate Democrats, 1 of 40 Senate Republicans, and the Senate's sole Independent.
The bill never advanced past committee referral, so none of its provisions—public financing, broadcast rules, or FEC filing changes—were ever debated or voted on by either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent senators and the large donors who fund their campaigns kept the existing private financing system, and broadcasters avoided the mandated advertising discounts. The general public did not get the reform.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor and Senate Assistant Majority Leader
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Elections Now Act and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Joined Durbin in introducing the bill as its lead Republican cosponsor.

for.name: Common Cause and other campaign reform groups
for.role: Public interest organizations backing public campaign financing
for.what_they_did: Publicly promoted the Fair Elections Now Act and pushed Congress to take it up.

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; sole referral destination
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing, reported it out, or allowed it to move toward a floor vote during the entire 111th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was lopsidedly Democratic—22 of 58 Democrats and the one Independent joined, versus just 1 of 40 Republicans—and with no committee or floor action ever taken, the bill's fate rested with the majority-run Rules Committee.

industries.note: Stations would have had to sell Senate candidate ads at up to 20% below the lowest unit charge, accept public vouchers as payment, never preempt paid candidate ads, and face license revocation for denying candidate access—while new FCC reporting would expose their political ad sales. The bill's voucher purchases would have brought them some new revenue, but the mandatory discounts and compliance burdens dominate.

The bill recommended a 0.5% tax on payments under federal contracts over $10 million (capped at $500,000 per year) to finance the campaign fund—a direct cost to major contractors, though as a non-binding provision it was not guaranteed.

industries.industry: Large campaign donors and lobbying firms
industries.note: Participating candidates would refuse contributions above small-dollar limits, bar joint fundraising committees, and face tighter coordinated-spending limits for party committees, shrinking the influence of big money on Senate campaigns.
